questions.q: Why, specifically, did the pre-sale load test fail to catch the availability-zone imbalance?
options: The load test used the wrong application code
The load test ran against a fixed-size node pool with no cluster-autoscaler activity, so it never exercised the live scaling event that produced the skew
The load test wasn't run long enough in minutes
The load test used a different Kubernetes version than production
questions.explain: Production's real autoscaling event — new nodes added mid-sale, each triggering a fresh scheduler bin-packing decision with no AZ-awareness — had no equivalent in the test's static node count.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a credible answer to Dana's question, 'how do we know there isn't a similar blind spot somewhere else'?
options: A promise that it will never happen again
What's already fixed and proven, what's now visible if it recurs, and a specific, scoped audit of the broader class of bug still being done
Just the root cause of the one incident
An apology and a request for more budget
questions.explain: A credible answer names the fix, the new visibility (the per-AZ dashboard panel), and a concrete next step — not a vague reassurance.

questions.q: What is the actual 'class' of blind spot Theo identifies as worth auditing platform-wide, beyond this one incident?
options: Any dashboard written in Grafana instead of Azure Monitor
Any cluster-wide average metric sitting on top of a dimension that can itself be imbalanced, such as per-AZ, per-node, or per-tenant
Any Kubernetes deployment older than six months
Any metric that isn't tagged for cost allocation
questions.explain: The real lesson wasn't 'Kubernetes scheduling is risky' — it was that any aggregate hiding an imbalanced underlying dimension can mask the same kind of problem.

questions.q: Why would telling Dana 'no, this was the only blind spot' have been the wrong answer, even if it made the meeting end more cleanly?
options: Because Dana would have believed it anyway
Because it would be a guess dressed up as confidence, and would erode trust the next time something breaks somewhere that guess didn't cover
Because Casey would have disagreed out loud
Because it's against company policy to answer leadership questions directly
questions.explain: A confident-sounding guess that turns out wrong later is more damaging to trust than an honest 'here's what's fixed, here's what's being checked.'

questions.q: What makes the FinOps dashboard's new per-AZ panel relevant to answering Dana's question, not just Casey's?
options: It proves the incident is fully forgotten
The same dashboard that missed the imbalance by averaging across AZs now makes a future imbalance visible as three uneven bars instead of one flat average
It has nothing to do with Dana's question
It replaced the need for any further auditing
questions.explain: The per-AZ panel directly answers part of 'is this still a blind spot' — the specific dashboard that hid the problem now can't hide the same kind of problem again.
